title: Generative AI Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Generative AI lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Creating a new sample
entries.summary: Generative AI creates an output using patterns learned during training. It can produce a new sentence or picture, but the result still needs checking.

example.code:
Request: write a two-line story about a kite
Possible output: A red kite rose above the field. Its string tugged gently in Mira's hand.
Check: two sentences, a kite, and a clear setting

notes: Newly generated text is not automatically true, original in every phrase, or suitable for every use.

entries.name: Learning and generating differ
entries.summary: Training changes a model using examples. Generation uses an already prepared model to produce an output. Asking a question is not the same operation as retraining all its weights.

example.code:
Training: adjust model numbers using many examples
Generation: use current model numbers and a new request
Review: inspect the generated result

notes: Do not assume a chat message instantly teaches every user's copy of a model.

entries.name: A toy word chooser
entries.summary: A language model predicts possible next pieces of text. This tiny list only illustrates choosing a next word; it is not a trained language model.

example.code:
choices = [("flies", 6), ("rests", 3), ("sings", 1)]
word = max(choices, key=lambda item: item[1])[0]
print("The kite", word)

notes: Hand-written scores in a list do not recreate how a large model learns language.

entries.name: Text can sound right and be wrong
entries.summary: A model can produce a believable statement that is false. This is often called a hallucination. Smooth writing is not evidence that a fact is correct.

example.code:
Generated claim: the school library opens at 7 AM
Known information: no opening time was supplied
Better response: the opening time is not provided

notes: Do not invent a citation or opening time to make an answer feel complete.

entries.name: Ground an answer in source text
entries.summary: Grounding means tying an answer to supplied evidence. The answer should stay within what that evidence supports.

example.code:
Source: The garden club meets on Friday in Room 4.
Task: When does the club meet? Use only the source.
Supported answer: Friday.

notes: A source can itself be outdated or wrong; grounding helps trace claims but does not prove the source is true.

entries.name: Picture prompts describe visible things
entries.summary: A picture request should describe the subject, setting and useful visual details. A model may miss a detail, so inspect the image afterward.

example.code:
Subject: one paper boat
Setting: a shallow puddle after rain
Style: simple coloured-pencil drawing
Check: one boat, readable shape, no unwanted text

notes: Generated pictures can miscount objects or distort details; count and inspect them yourself.

entries.name: Diffusion starts from noise
entries.summary: Many image models use diffusion. In a simplified view, generation starts with noise and repeatedly changes it toward a picture guided by a request.

example.code:
Start: random-looking pixels
Repeated step: predict and reduce noise using the model
Guide: description of a paper boat
End: a candidate picture to inspect

notes: Not every image model uses exactly this process.

entries.name: Sound requests need timing
entries.summary: Generated audio may include speech, music or effects. A useful request names the length and purpose so the result can fit its setting.

example.code:
Task: a short bell effect for a lesson timer
Length: about one second
Character: gentle and easy to hear
Check: no sudden loud peak; clear start and end

notes: Do not imitate a real person's voice without suitable permission.

entries.name: Generated code needs a test
entries.summary: Code from a model is a proposed solution. Read it and check examples, including small edge cases, before using it.
notes: Do not run unfamiliar code with private files or powerful permissions just to see what it does.

entries.name: Variation is part of generation
entries.summary: Some generation methods choose among several possible outputs. A seed can help repeat a run, but exact repeatability also depends on tools and settings.

example.code:
Request: name a friendly robot
Candidate A: Piko
Candidate B: Nori
Review: easy to read, fits the character, check existing uses before publishing

notes: A chosen seed does not guarantee identical output across every model version or device.

entries.name: Evaluate with a small checklist
entries.summary: Evaluation is a planned check of the result. Include the task rules and the mistakes that would matter to the user.

example.code:
Task: explain rain to a young reader
Check 1: uses short familiar sentences
Check 2: explains clouds and water drops accurately
Check 3: avoids made-up facts
Check 4: answers the actual question

notes: Do not score only the examples you liked; include difficult cases too.

entries.name: Use outputs with care
entries.summary: Before sharing generated work, review facts, privacy, permissions and suitability. Keep a person responsible for the final choice.

example.code:
Before sharing a poster:
Check names and dates
Use permitted source material
Remove private details
Read all visible text
Say how AI helped when that context matters

notes: A tool allowing a download does not settle every reuse right or factual question.
